title: Floppy disk
wiki_lead:
A floppy disk, diskette, or floppy diskette is a type of disk storage made from a thin, flexible disk coated with a magnetic storage medium. It is enclosed in a square or nearly square plastic shell lined with fabric to help remove dust from the spinning disk. Floppy disks store digital data, which can be read or written when inserted into a floppy disk drive (FDD) connected to or built into a computer or other device. The three most popular types of floppy disks (and their drives) are the 8-inch, 5¼-inch, and 3½-inch versions.
The first floppy disks, invented and made by IBM in 1971, had a disk diameter of 8 inches. Subsequently, the 5¼-inch and then the 3½-inch became a ubiquitous form of data storage and data transfer into the first years of the 21st century. By the end of the 1980s, 5¼-inch disks had been superseded by 3½-inch disks. During this time, PCs frequently came equipped with drives of both sizes. By the mid-1990s, 5¼-inch drives had nearly disappeared, the 3½-inch disk became the dominant format. The advantages of the 3½-inch disk are its higher capacity, smaller physical size, and rigid case which provided better protection from dirt and other environmental risks.
Floppy disks were so common in late 20th-century culture that many electronic and software programs continue to use save icons that look like floppy disks well into the 21st century, as a form of skeuomorphic design. While floppy disk drives still have some limited uses, especially with legacy industrial computer equipment, they have been superseded by data storage methods with much greater data storage capacity and data transfer speed, such as USB flash drives, memory cards, optical discs, and storage available through local computer networks and cloud storage.

Categories

Industry observers categorize floppy disks and floppy disk drives according to size and capacity with four major categories being 8 inches (200 mm), 5.25 inches (130 mm), 3.5 inches (90 mm) and high-capacity floppy disks and floppy disk drives.
There were in addition, variant products that did not fit these categories.  The distinguishing characteristic between the high-capacity products and their lower capacity brethren, frequently categorized as standard floppies, was the use of servomechanisms to increase the number of tracks and thereby increase capacity.
The four categories each represented generations; from the beginning each generation had substantially greater market success and ultimately succeeded the previous one, but the high-capacity floppy generation, although having some success, was never as successful as the prior 3½-inch (90 mm) generation, and became essentially obsolete by 2011.
While the original IBM 8-inch (200 mm) disk was actually so defined, the other sizes are defined in millimeters, their names being but rough approximations.

grok_lead: A floppy disk is a magnetic storage medium consisting of a thin, flexible disk made of Mylar coated with iron oxide for data recording, enclosed in a protective square jacket that includes a fabric liner to clean the disk surface during use. A floppy disk cannot be used as an input device. It is a passive magnetic storage medium used to store digital data. Input devices (e.g., keyboards, mice, scanners) actively send data or control signals to a computer. While a floppy disk drive reads data from the disk (providing input to the computer) and writes data to it (output), the floppy disk itself is classified as storage media, not an input device. It functions by spinning the disk at high speed while read/write heads in a floppy disk drive access concentric tracks on its surface to store or retrieve binary data. Invented by IBM engineers in 1967 and first commercially introduced in 1971, the floppy disk revolutionized data handling by replacing cumbersome punched cards and magnetic tapes with a portable, removable format. The original 8-inch floppy disk, with a capacity of about 80 kilobytes (equivalent to roughly 3,000 punched cards), was developed for loading microcode into IBM mainframe computers like the System/370. Subsequent formats included the 5Â¼-inch "minifloppy" introduced in 1976 by Shugart Associates, which offered capacities up to 1.2 megabytes in high-density versions and became standard in personal computers such as the Apple II (1977) and IBM PC (1981). The 3Â½-inch disk, launched by Sony in 1981 and popularized in 1986, featured a rigid plastic shell with a metal shutter for better durability and contamination resistance, achieving a standard capacity of 1.44 megabytes in high-density models. By the mid-1990s, annual production reached 5 billion units, underscoring its ubiquity in the personal computing era. Floppy disks served as the primary method for distributing software, creating backups, and transferring files between computers until the late 1990s, enabling the growth of the software industry and hobbyist computing through operating systems like CP/M. However, their limitationsâlow storage capacity relative to growing file sizes, vulnerability to physical damage, and slow access speedsâled to obsolescence by the mid-2000s, supplanted by CD-ROMs, DVDs, USB flash drives, and cloud storage. Despite this, floppy disks retain niche uses in legacy systems, such as industrial controls and certain aircraft avionics, where reliability in outdated environments persists.
